units.text: 11. Will Books Die? The Question Needs Unpacking
The Market Can Grow While Reading Retreats

“The book is dying” can mean at least three different things: volumes are no longer published or bought; substantial works are replaced by other forms; sustained reading becomes a rare practice. The first is a statement about the market, the second about culture, the third about behavior and access. They can develop differently. An industry can sell well to part of the population while the practice contracts in other groups.

Data published by the Association of American Publishers on August 10, 2026, estimate United States revenue of 33.4 billion dollars in 2025 from books and course materials in print and digital formats. Print accounted for 76.3% of revenue in the general-interest book segment. These are American industry estimates, not a global measure of reading or a measure of the time spent with each volume. Even so, they do not describe an industry that has disappeared. [ 22 ]

On a different measure, a study presented by UCL in August 2025, based on the American Time Use Survey, shows a decline in the proportion of people reading for pleasure on an average day: from 28% in 2004 to 16% in 2023. The category also included digital formats and listening to audiobooks. This is not the percentage of people who read at least one book in a year. The study is observational and does not establish the cause of the decline. [ 21 ]

The two findings do not cancel each other out. Money and time measure different things. Revenue can be influenced by prices, product types, and the concentration of purchases. A purchased copy may be read by several people or by none. A borrowed book may matter without appearing as a new sale. We cannot move from one indicator to the other as though they were synonyms.

In June 2026, the Audio Publishers Association reported 9% growth in audiobook revenue for 2025 in its market research. The estimate has its own methodology and should not be mechanically combined with AAP figures. It is nevertheless a sign that a work in audio form can offer a direction for commercial growth, not merely a hypothesis about the future. [ 23 ]

These American data do not authorize identical claims about Romania, Switzerland, or the whole world. We use them to show how the vitality of some segments can coexist with serious reasons for concern about the practice. A local analysis would need its own data and comparable definitions. A book about the future becomes more credible when it refuses to turn one country into the planet.

The real question is what we want to survive. Is it enough for expensive editions, beautiful collections, and a passionate community to exist? From the perspective of the object, perhaps. From the perspective of a society in which people have access to substantial arguments and can discuss shared texts, no. Survival as a luxury good is not the same as the vitality of a shared practice.

A book culture also needs work that is hard to see in the cover price: selection, editing, translation, verification, preservation, and guidance. If producing text becomes very cheap, these functions do not disappear by definition. On the contrary, in a scenario of abundance, readers may have an even greater need to know who checked it, how errors were corrected, and why a particular work deserves their time.

It does not follow that existing economic models should be frozen in place. Some can restrict access; others can support the necessary work. The question is how we pay for real value without confusing the difficulty of distribution with intellectual merit. A file may be easy to copy, while writing a good book remains demanding work. An abundance of copies does not imply an abundance of judgment.
Four Futures, None Inevitable

The first scenario is selective retreat. Books used mainly for specific answers lose ground to faster tools, while the novel, the carefully constructed essay, and some syntheses remain attractive. This would not be the death of the book, but a redistribution of its functions. Some losses might be healthy. A volume that hides a single idea among many repetitions has no natural right to the reader’s time.

But a risk arises here too. An introductory book may look like a collection of simple answers, although its value lies in the order that connects them. If we replace it with isolated answers, we may save minutes and lose the framework that allows us to ask better questions. In this scenario, the challenge is to distinguish useful compression from the amputation of structure.

The second scenario is the book as a privileged refuge. Part of the public retains the time and space for reading, while everyone else mainly receives fragmented content, quick guidance, and answers on demand. I am not claiming that this is the proven future. I consider it a risk to take seriously, because preserving the object does not guarantee that the conditions for access are shared. A world with splendid libraries and little free time can be deeply unequal in the way it allows people to think.

The third scenario is good hybridization. The work has a stable core, but can be read, listened to, annotated, and discussed. A video demonstration appears where it explains something real. The assistant answers when called and stays quiet otherwise. Readers can see what belongs to the author, what is a correction, and what is an automated interpretation. In this scenario, the book survives through an adaptation that preserves its identity, rather than despite adaptation.

The fourth scenario is abundance without guidance. Producing volumes that look convincing becomes easy, but their quality varies, and verification remains costly. Readers no longer lack text; they lack sound reasons for choosing. The answer need not be an automatic return to a few closed editorial gates. It can be the construction of more transparent mechanisms for review, provenance, correction, and recommendation.

These scenarios can combine. A book can be hybrid and financially inaccessible. An open project can be thoroughly checked. A printed edition can contain careless text. A conversational service can encourage reading or replace it with tailored answers. The medium alone does not determine the distribution of quality and power.

Who stands to gain depends on the configuration. Authors can reach new readers through accessible formats. Readers can reduce barriers of language and navigation. Intermediaries can create value through selection and verification, or capture the relationship with the public without assuming the same responsibility. Libraries can become more important as spaces for access and guidance, but only if they have the necessary resources.

For society, the stakes go beyond the existence of a cultural product. They concern the possibility of having shared objects of discussion. If each person receives a different, continually adapted reformulation, what exactly are we criticizing together? Personalization can be useful, but it should preserve a text and a version we can return to. Without a shared object, disagreement risks becoming a conversation between summaries that do not match.

My prediction is therefore conditional: books have strong reasons to continue, but the shape of their success is not guaranteed. I would bet on transformation and differentiation before total disappearance. Yet I would not comfortably bet that sustained reading will remain accessible to everyone without institutional effort. The future depends on more than how good books are. It also depends on what kind of life leaves people time to enter them.
